title: the twins fall
hookLine: the twins fall next, the wise one and the beautiful one, and the reason given is the same small sentence twice
carry: amanitva: keep the gift, drop the ranking
tomorrow: Arjuna falls, then Bhima. what were the strongest brothers carrying?

cards: Sahadeva and Nakula are the youngest of the five, the twins, sons of Madri, raised by Kunti as her own.

In this serial they have often stood just behind their older brothers: Sahadeva, known for his learning; Nakula, known as the handsome one. Now, on the road toward Meru, Sahadeva falls. A little later, Nakula falls too.
Both times Bhima calls out to the front of the line, and both times Yudhishthira answers without stopping.

teach.b: Listen to the shape of the answers. About Sahadeva, in Ganguli's telling: he thought no one was equal to him in wisdom.
About Nakula: he thought no one was equal to him in beauty. The same sentence twice, with one word changed. Look at what isn't blamed.
Not the learning. Not the good looks. Those are gifts, and the epic has praised both brothers for them.
What trips each of them is a small private thought laid on top of the gift: no one is equal to me. Sahadeva's wisdom could have walked on with him.
What he couldn't carry to the top of the world, in this telling, was the comparison. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: AMANITVA: FIRST ON THE GITA'S LIST
teach.b: In the Gita, when Krishna lists what real knowledge looks like, the very first word is amanitva: humility, literally not thinking much of yourself.
Sahadeva, the learned one, had the knowledge and missed the first item on the list. Notice he never said it out loud.
Hindu teaching counts the private ranking too, the quiet no one is equal to me, because that's where pride lives first. Behind the line, the dog still walks.
Three travelers are left with Yudhishthira now: Bhima, Arjuna and the dog. The road narrows as the people on it fall away.

how: The falls of Sahadeva and Nakula are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva, and Hindu teachers sometimes set them beside the Gita's list of the marks of knowledge, which begins with humility.

o: the youngest Pandava, a twin known for his learning
a son Kunti bore to the wind god before Arjuna
the Pandavas' charioteer on the last journey

games.q: the twins fall — tap the pairs.
p: none equal to him in wisdom
none equal to him in beauty

s: Yudhishthira blames the twins' learning and looks
the gifts aren't blamed; the fault named is thinking no one their equal.
Yudhishthira's two answers have the same shape
the same sentence, with wisdom swapped for beauty.
humility is the first mark of knowledge on the Gita's list
Gita 13: Krishna's list of what knowledge looks like begins with amanitva, humility.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. Bhima asks why your learned youngest brother has fallen. what reason do you give?
o: he wasn't strong enough for the road.
he thought no one equal to him in wisdom.
games.why: Yudhishthira says Sahadeva thought no one his equal in wisdom, and gives the same answer for Nakula and beauty.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're genuinely good at, without modesty, and breathe in simply glad of it.
Breathe out and notice whether a second thought comes attached, a comparison, a ranking, someone you're better than; if it does, set that thought down and keep the gift.
If you pray, thank God for the gift by name; if you don't, simply be glad of it.

wordCard.voice: Sahadeva. The youngest Pandava, known for his wisdom, who falls on the road for thinking no one his equal in it.

orig.note: Sahadeva: the youngest Pandava, known for his learning, who falls second.

carryVoice: Your line: amanitva, keep the gift, drop the ranking. The gift was never the problem. That's day eight hundred seventy-five.
